content: Prehospital systems are structured to ensure that individuals in need of urgent medical care can access the healthcare system promptly, safely, and effectively. These systems must be tailored to the specific needs of the local population, taking into account factors such as cultural norms, legal frameworks, infrastructure, healthcare capacity, economic considerations, and administrative resources. By doing so, countries can optimize the use of their existing infrastructure and local expertise. To prevent redundancy or unnecessary competition, it is advisable to integrate existing regional health-service administrative structures whenever feasible. At the regional level, an administrator should be designated to oversee the training, operations, reporting, and quality assurance activities of local prehospital systems within their jurisdiction. Community leaders and members of the population being served should be actively involved in the development and administration of these systems. Their insights, suggestions, and participation in the design process are invaluable, as the definition of a community member may vary across different regions. The financing of emergency care systems differs globally. For instance, in Mexico, most prehospital care providers are affiliated with voluntary or nonprofit organizations, whereas in Karachi, Pakistan, the majority work for profit-driven businesses, with some employed by nonprofit entities. In other countries, municipal or governmental funding supports these systems. Regardless of the model, the administration of prehospital trauma care systems requires identifying a lead organization to ensure safe and effective operations. Leadership at both national and regional levels is critical for system development and public education about its use. A lead agency should be established to oversee the implementation and management of the system, including its financing. In some nations, this role is assumed by the Ministry of Health, while in others, it may fall under the Ministry of Interior or Transportation. Once the foundational framework is in place, creating a dedicated agency to manage the prehospital system on an ongoing basis should be considered. This agency would also coordinate prehospital care at the local level, leveraging hospital-based facilities, training equipment, and data for quality assurance. At the community or regional level, various approaches have been employed to develop, organize, and regulate prehospital systems. The chosen model often determines which individual or agency is best suited to administer the system, including responsibilities such as personnel hiring, system financing, provider training, quality assurance audits, communication management, medical oversight, logistical support, and operational supervision. Common models include national systems managed by central governmental authorities, private systems operated by emergency medical service companies (either nonprofit or for-profit), and hospital-based systems, which are particularly prevalent in rural and remote areas. Medical direction is a cornerstone of prehospital care systems. At the local level, a knowledgeable and dedicated healthcare professional should serve as the medical director. In urban areas, this role is best filled by an experienced hospital-based physician trained in emergency medicine, anesthesiology, critical care, or trauma surgery, ideally with prehospital care experience. In rural areas where physicians may not be available, the most experienced nurse or paramedic should assume this role. The medical director is responsible for recruiting and training care teams, conducting needs assessments, overseeing continuing education, developing clinical protocols, participating in quality improvement efforts, reviewing reports, providing feedback, and conducting critical-incident debriefings. The importance of securing a capable and motivated medical director to oversee clinical operations cannot be overstated. Disaster planning is an essential component of any prehospital care system, regardless of its size, budget, or location. Local agencies, governments, and organizations must prepare for large-scale natural disasters or man-made incidents that could result in mass casualties. A disaster planning document should aim to strengthen the capacity of local and regional governments, healthcare providers, and public health organizations to respond effectively. Establishing a robust and sustainable emergency system is the best way to prepare for such events. Financial considerations are critical in prehospital trauma care. Access to potentially life-saving services should not be restricted to those who can afford them. However, cost recovery mechanisms, such as health insurance or public funding, may be necessary to ensure the system's financial viability. Care should never be withheld due to a patient’s inability to pay at the time of service, nor should fear of treatment costs deter individuals from seeking care. Innovative strategies, such as allocating portions of highway construction budgets, vehicle registration fees, traffic fines, or fuel taxes, may help generate resources for prehospital systems. Political support is vital for the operational and financial sustainability of prehospital systems. Emergency care services require the engagement of community, political, and governmental leaders who are willing to draft enabling legislation, secure funding, and support local medical directors in improving care quality and availability. A lack of political support, corruption, or administrative infighting can undermine even the best efforts of prehospital care personnel. Medical professionals should educate the public and key officials about the importance of prehospital care, leveraging their credibility and influence to advocate for the system. Legislation and regulation play a crucial role in prehospital trauma care systems. These frameworks ensure public health and safety, clarify the roles and responsibilities of agencies and individuals, and promote consistent care and system responses nationwide. Topics commonly addressed by legislation include provider training, certification, and licensure; scope of practice; medical direction protocols; vehicle and equipment standards; quality improvement; financing; and disaster response. In countries lacking such legislation, prehospital care providers and physicians should collaborate to establish it. A case study from Thailand illustrates the development and implementation of a prehospital care system. Recognizing the need for effective prehospital care, the Ministry of Public Health adopted a long-term strategic plan in 1994, implemented in three phases. Key components included administration and management, personnel development, ambulance standards, and communication systems. Despite significant progress, challenges remain, such as establishing national legislation, developing a central alarm center, setting national standards for personnel, and implementing a sustainable budget system. In summary, prehospital care systems require careful planning, robust leadership, community involvement, financial sustainability, political support, and legislative frameworks to ensure their effectiveness and resilience.
